summary: A monthly report of ARPANET traffic for November 1973. It tabulates, for each Host, how many packets it sent, split between traffic that stayed within its own node and traffic sent to other nodes, with daily averages. It is a data memo and defines no protocol.

eli5.summary: It is like a monthly count of how many cars used each road, written down so people can see which roads are busy.

questions: how much traffic did the arpanet carry in november 1973
subtitle: A snapshot of ARPANET traffic volume across all hosts in November 1973

tldr.problem: ARPANET operators need to understand how much traffic flows through the network and which hosts send the most data, to monitor health and plan capacity.
tldr.mechanism: McKenzie at BBN collects monthly statistics from each host, counting packets sent both within a node (intra-node) and between nodes (inter-node), then publishes the data as a simple table.
tldr.outcome: This becomes a monthly reporting tradition that provides the first systematic view of network usage. The data shows that by late 1973, the network carries over 85 million inter-node packets per month, with heavy users like ISI and AMES far exceeding lighter traffic sites.

today: RFC 601 is a historical data snapshot, one of the first published traffic reports for any computer network. The monthly traffic reporting tradition it began—monitoring packet volume, identifying heavy users, and publishing the data—remains fundamental to network operations today.

sections.title: ARPANET Traffic Statistics
sections.content: This RFC publishes the first public record of ARPANET traffic volume for a single month: November 1973. It tabulates, for each connected host, how many packets it transmitted, split between traffic destined for other hosts (inter-node) and traffic within the same node (intra-node). Each host typically operated multiple machines, so the data is broken down by individual host identity. The report includes daily averages, allowing readers to understand traffic patterns across a month.
sections.eli5: This is a monthly count of how many data packets each computer on the ARPANET sent, listed so people can see which sites were busiest.

sections.title: Traffic Distribution
sections.content: The data reveals stark differences in traffic volume. ISI Host 1 was by far the heaviest user, sending 11.2 million inter-node packets. Other heavy users included Ames Host 0 (3.5 million), XEROX Host 1 (9.7 million intra-node but none inter-node), and several others in the millions. The lightest sites, like BELV, sent only a few thousand packets. In total, the network carried approximately 85 million inter-node packets and 24 million intra-node packets in November, for an average of 2.8 million packets per day. The ratio of total packets to messages was 1.08, indicating that most messages arrived intact in a single packet.
sections.eli5: Some computers sent hundreds of millions of packets (the big research centers), others sent thousands (the small sites). The network as a whole handled about 85 million inter-node packets in the month.

sections.title: Significance
sections.content: This monthly traffic summary establishes a baseline for ARPANET operations in late 1973, about four years after the network's inception. The data shows a mature, active network with substantial traffic from research institutions, particularly ISI, Ames, and Stanford. The relatively low ratio of packets to messages (1.08) indicates the network was working well—most messages needed just one packet. This RFC begins a tradition of monthly traffic reporting that would inform network planning and operations decisions for years.
sections.eli5: By 1973, ARPANET was healthy and busy, with lots of research centers actively using it. This count showed the network was ready for more growth.
